paragraphs.text: A rolled [Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) from Anxi, made in 1995 and kept for thirty-one years since. It was made in the decade when the newer light, green style began to take over in Anxi. Tieguanyin held this long counts as a style of its own, which the trade calls chenxiang, or [old Tie](tieguanyin:styles). The light style goes stale fast, so the tea set aside for years is usually the heavier [charcoal roasted](tieguanyin:ageing) kind, kept sealed, dry, dark and cool, away from strong smells.

[Anxi](anxi:where-it-is) is a county of Quanzhou in southern Fujian, on the southern side of the Daiyun mountains, and the trade names Xiping township there as the place this tea began. The county was still one of the poorer in the province until the 1990s, when the [Tieguanyin boom](anxi:history) changed that. The tea was rolled into its tight balls by [wrapping it in cloth](tieguanyin:making), pressing it and drying it a little, then wrapping it again, several times over, each round tightening the leaf.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, rounder, softer cup with the fire gone, a liquor turned orange-red or reddish-brown, and often a soft fruity sourness.
